meta.titre: Pulleys: velocity ratio, mechanical advantage and efficiency

sections.contenu_markdown: At a building site in Douala, a worker raises sacks of cement to the first floor with a rope running over a wheel, instead of climbing the stairs with each sack. A garage mechanic lifts a car engine with a chain hoist that has several wheels. These are pulley systems: they let a small pull lift a big load, at the price of pulling the rope over a longer distance. The GCE O/L asks for the velocity ratio, mechanical advantage and efficiency of such systems.

items: Work done equals force times distance moved in the direction of the force, $W = Fd$, in joules.
A machine makes work easier by changing the size or the direction of a force.
The load is the force the machine overcomes; the effort is the force the user applies.

sections.titre: Pulley systems: MA, VR and efficiency
sections.contenu_markdown:
A **pulley** is a grooved wheel that carries a rope. A **block and tackle** is a combination of fixed and movable pulleys.

Three quantities describe a pulley system:

- **Mechanical advantage (MA)** $= \dfrac{\text{load}}{\text{effort}}$. It has no unit.
- **Velocity ratio (VR)** $= \dfrac{\text{distance moved by the effort}}{\text{distance moved by the load}}$. For a pulley system, VR equals the **number of rope sections supporting the movable block** (the strands that pull the lower block upward).
- **Efficiency** $= \dfrac{\text{MA}}{\text{VR}} \times 100\% = \dfrac{\text{work done on the load}}{\text{work done by the effort}} \times 100\%$.

| System | VR | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Single fixed pulley | 1 | only changes the direction of the force |
| Single movable pulley | 2 | halves the effort (ideally) |
| Block and tackle with $n$ supporting strands | $n$ | effort reduced $n$ times (ideally) |

In an ideal machine MA $=$ VR and the efficiency is $100\%$. In a real machine friction in the pulleys and the weight of the movable block and the rope take part of the work, so MA $<$ VR and the efficiency is below $100\%$. The work done by the effort is always greater than the work obtained on the load: a pulley system never gives you more work, only a smaller force over a larger distance.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a diagram or text describes the arrangement of ropes and pulleys.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Count only the rope sections that pull the **lower (movable) block** upward. The end of the rope where the effort is applied counts as a supporting strand only if it leaves the movable block; if it leaves a fixed pulley it does not count. Do not simply count wheels. Check with distances: if the effort moves $4\ \mathrm{m}$ while the load rises $1\ \mathrm{m}$, then VR $= 4$.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When distances and forces for the effort and the load are given.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Work done by the effort $= E \times d_E$ and work done on the load $= L \times d_L$. Then $\text{efficiency} = \dfrac{L d_L}{E d_E} \times 100\%$. The difference between the two quantities of work is the energy wasted, mainly by friction and by lifting the movable block. To increase efficiency: oil the pulleys, use light movable blocks and light rope.

sections.enonce_markdown: A block and tackle has $4$ rope sections supporting the movable block. An effort of $200\ \mathrm{N}$ raises a load of $600\ \mathrm{N}$ through $0.50\ \mathrm{m}$. Calculate (a) the velocity ratio, (b) the mechanical advantage, (c) the efficiency and (d) the work done by the effort.

etapes.justification: VR equals the number of rope sections supporting the movable block.
MA is load divided by effort.
Efficiency is MA divided by VR, as a percentage.

etapes.action: Find the distance moved by the effort.
etapes.justification: The effort moves VR times the distance moved by the load.

etapes.action: Calculate the work done by the effort, and check the efficiency.
etapes.justification: Work $= Fd$; the work done on the load is $600 \times 0.50$.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Work by effort $= 200 \times 2.0 = 400\ \mathrm{J}$; work on load $= 600 \times 0.50 = 300\ \mathrm{J}$; $\dfrac{300}{400} \times 100 = 75\%$

sections.conclusion_markdown: VR = **4**, MA = **3**, efficiency = **75 %**, and the effort does **400 J** of work, of which **300 J** is useful.

items.erreur_markdown: A student counts every pulley in the diagram as one unit of velocity ratio, so that a system with 2 fixed and 2 movable pulleys is given VR = 4 without checking the rope.
items.pourquoi_faux: The velocity ratio is the number of rope sections supporting the movable block, not the number of wheels.
items.correction_markdown: Count the strands that pull on the lower block; verify by comparing the distance moved by the effort and by the load.

items.erreur_markdown: A student writes: "The machine has an MA of 4, so it has an efficiency of 4."
items.pourquoi_faux: Efficiency is a percentage found from MA divided by VR (or output work over input work). It is not equal to the MA.

items.erreur_markdown: A student calculates an efficiency of 120 % and writes it as the final answer.
items.pourquoi_faux: No machine can give out more work than is put in, so the efficiency is always below 100 %. The ratio has been inverted.
items.correction_markdown: Put the work done on the load (output) on top and the work by the effort (input) at the bottom.

items.erreur_markdown: A student says that the pulley system saves work because the effort is smaller than the load.
items.pourquoi_faux: The effort is smaller, but it moves through a larger distance. The work by the effort is at least as large as the work on the load.
items.correction_markdown: Say that the system reduces the force needed but not the work: $E \times d_E \geq L \times d_L$.

items.enonce_markdown: A single movable pulley lifts a load of $80\ \mathrm{N}$ when an effort of $50\ \mathrm{N}$ is applied. Calculate (a) the mechanical advantage and (b) the efficiency of the pulley.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\text{MA} = \dfrac{\text{load}}{\text{effort}} = \dfrac{80}{50} = 1.6$. **MA = 1.6.**

(b) A single movable pulley has two supporting sections, so $\text{VR} = 2$. $\text{efficiency} = \dfrac{1.6}{2} \times 100 = 80\%$. **Efficiency = 80 %.**

items.enonce_markdown: A pulley system with a velocity ratio of $3$ is used to raise a load of $450\ \mathrm{N}$ through a height of $2.0\ \mathrm{m}$. The effort needed is $200\ \mathrm{N}$. Calculate (a) the mechanical advantage, (b) the distance moved by the effort, (c) the work done by the effort and by the load, (d) the efficiency and (e) the energy wasted.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\text{MA} = \dfrac{450}{200} = 2.25$.

(b) $d_E = \text{VR} \times d_L = 3 \times 2.0 = 6.0\ \mathrm{m}$.

(c) Work by effort $= 200 \times 6.0 = 1\,200\ \mathrm{J}$. Work on load $= 450 \times 2.0 = 900\ \mathrm{J}$.

(d) Efficiency $= \dfrac{900}{1\,200} \times 100 = 75\%$. Check: $\dfrac{2.25}{3} \times 100 = 75\%$.

(e) Energy wasted $= 1\,200 - 900 = 300\ \mathrm{J}$.

**MA = 2.25; effort moves 6.0 m; work by effort 1200 J, on load 900 J; efficiency 75 %; 300 J wasted.**

items.enonce_markdown: A pulley system has a velocity ratio of $5$ and an efficiency of $80\%$. (a) Calculate its mechanical advantage. (b) What effort is needed to raise a load of $1000\ \mathrm{N}$? (c) A man of weight $600\ \mathrm{N}$ pulls the rope downward. What is the largest load, and its mass, that he could raise, if the efficiency stays the same? Take $g = 10\ \mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$. (d) What length of rope must he pull in to raise the load by $1.2\ \mathrm{m}$?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\text{efficiency} = \dfrac{\text{MA}}{\text{VR}} \times 100$, so $\text{MA} = \dfrac{80}{100} \times 5 = 4$. **MA = 4.**

(b) $\text{effort} = \dfrac{\text{load}}{\text{MA}} = \dfrac{1000}{4} = 250\ \mathrm{N}$. **Effort = 250 N.**

(c) The man cannot pull down with more than his own weight, so the greatest effort is $600\ \mathrm{N}$. Load $= \text{MA} \times \text{effort} = 4 \times 600 = 2\,400\ \mathrm{N}$, and the mass is $\dfrac{2\,400}{10} = 240\ \mathrm{kg}$. **Largest load = 2 400 N (240 kg).**

(d) Length of rope $= \text{VR} \times 1.2 = 5 \times 1.2 = 6.0\ \mathrm{m}$. **Rope pulled in = 6.0 m.**

items_markdown: $\text{MA} = \dfrac{\text{load}}{\text{effort}}$ and $\text{VR} = \dfrac{d_E}{d_L}$ = number of rope sections supporting the movable block.
A fixed pulley only changes the direction of the force (VR = 1); a movable pulley has VR = 2.
Friction and the weight of the movable block make real pulley systems less than 100 % efficient, so MA is less than VR.
A pulley system reduces the force needed, but the effort moves farther and no work is saved.
